source.title: SafeGene: Reusable Adapters for Transferable Safety Alignment
source.authors: Yanghan Wang; Zhi Kou; Fu Feng; Jing Wang; Xin Geng

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present, though some table layout is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign downstream fine-tuning weakens safety using task-specific classification fine-tuning and harmful-response attack success rates, rather than the original study's fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for benign downstream fine-tuning and a layer-selection ablation. The 320 harmful examples used to construct the safety-degraded student are a setup detail; no harmful-fine-tuning safety outcome for that student is reported. Results cited from other work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-response ASR of five instruction-tuned models before and after LoRA fine-tuning on benign classification tasks (AG News, SST2, MNLI, BoolQ). This is a different benign-data setup aimed at the V2 question. Most of the paper is about the SafeGene recovery method, which is not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say downstream fine-tuning 'often' increases ASR (+7.70 points on average), not uniformly. Their main conclusion concerns SafeGene: it reduces ASR by 11.48 points versus fine-tuned models, preserves accuracy, and beats SafeLoRA, SafeMERGE and SaLoRA on the safety–utility trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates benign downstream task fine-tuning using classification and reasoning datasets, with harmful-instruction ASR as the safety measure; it does not reproduce the original study's specific fine-tuning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that layer-selection ratio affects outcomes: retaining 0.7 of the distilled safety vectors improves accuracy and lowers ASR, while further pruning hurts safety. It also evaluates Qwen2.5-7B with an auxiliary API judge.

fits_no_version.finding: Data-aware selection retaining 0.7 of SafeGene's distilled layer vectors lowers BeaverTails ASR vs random selection; more pruning hurts safety.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety recovery via distilled adapters benefits from selecting a subset of layers, but over-pruning degrades it.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. Safety is evaluated with automatic judges, and the authors note that judges can misclassify outputs. The evaluation is text-only and single-turn; the authors also note that recalibration uses target-domain safety data whose coverage may affect performance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were omitted. SafeGene recovery and baseline-method comparisons were not extracted as claim-version rows because they do not test the listed claims about fine-tuning-induced erosion, token-position concentration, bypasses, or safety localization.

untested.parts: Only LoRA fine-tuning on classification/reasoning datasets (9,000 examples) was tested. Benign instruction-tuning data such as Alpaca/Dolly, carefully selected benign data, and full-parameter fine-tuning were not tested.
The safety-degraded student is built from 320 harmful BeaverTails examples, but its harmful compliance is never reported.
Not tested. Layer selection concerns the distilled adapter, not the model's own weights.
Not tested. SafeGene is a post-hoc adapter, not a deepening method.

missing.what: Per-model base vs fine-tuned ASR (four-task average, BT/Adv/DR). Qwen2.5-7B 31.7→42.9; Qwen2.5-1.5B 41.0→51.0; Qwen3-1.7B 28.6→41.9; GLM-4-9B 23.1→23.7 (absent); Llama-3-8B 36.7→40.2 (partial).
Per-task fine-tuned ASR vs base. Fine-tuning lowers ASR below base for GLM-4-9B on AG News and for Llama-3-8B on BoolQ.

record.verdict_notes: Base models already show high ASR under Beaver-dam-7B (~32%), so the erosion is measured on top of a weak baseline. No uncertainty estimates are given. The study is not an original source. The reader's single 'supports' for the aggregate masks a null result on GLM-4-9B and a weak one on Llama-3-8B.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report harmful-response outcomes from fine-tuning on harmful examples.
Tests downstream classification-task fine-tuning on 9,000 examples per task; does not test other kinds of ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data.
No per-token KL divergence by response position is measured.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes are tested.
The layer-selection ablation concerns SafeGene's distilled adapter vectors, not whether a small set of the model's own weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test why safety behaviour is shallow or whether data or training objectives produce shallowness.
SafeGene is a safety-recovery adapter, but the study does not test training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens or whether such deepening holds up.

rows.subject: All five evaluated model families (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B, GLM-4-9B, and Llama-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on downstream task data; the study reports the aggregate comparison with the original aligned models.

conditions.value: AG News, SST2, MNLI, and BoolQ; 9,000 training examples per task
Average across five model families and four downstream tasks

rows.note: The text states that fine-tuning increases average ASR by 7.70%; it also gives the comparison as 32.21% to 39.91%.
rows.check: Values check against Table 1: base average (35.88+28.85+31.89)/3=32.21, fine-tuned (44.10+34.42+41.22)/3=39.91. The aggregate hides large per-model differences; see missing rows.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on downstream task data; compared with the original aligned model.

conditions.value: 200 sampled examples from each of BeaverTails, AdvBench, and DirectRefusal per task

rows.note: The paper reports 2,400 evaluations total across four tasks. SafeGene reduces the count to 11, but that adapter result is not the fine-tuning effect recorded in this row.
rows.check: 56 to 80 successful attacks out of 2,400 evaluations is about 2.3% to 3.3%. The relative rise is clear, but the absolute rates are an order of magnitude below the Beaver-dam ASRs. Effect size depends heavily on the judge.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Pruned the distilled SafeGene safety-vector bank using layer selection; the text describes the ratio 0.7 and says further pruning hurts safety.
rows.note: The text says a retained ratio of 0.7 lowers ASR, while further pruning hurts safety. This concerns SafeGene adapter vectors, not localization of safety in the model's original parameters.
rows.check: This is an ablation of the study's own adapter-vector pruning, shown only in a figure. It is the study's method, not a claim-version result; it should not carry a partial state.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B; Beaver-dam-7B judge; average over four tasks
relationships.reason: Three-benchmark ASR rises about 31.7→42.9, 41.0→51.0 and 28.6→41.9 (Table 1). These are missing per-model rows; verdict based on the text; aggregate in R1.
relationships.display_finding: Average attack success over three benchmarks rose from about 31.7 to 42.9, from 41.0 to 51.0 and from 28.6 to 41.9.

relationships.reason: ASR rises only about 36.7→40.2 on average. BoolQ fine-tuning gives ~34.1, below base (Table 1; missing row, verdict from text).
relationships.display_finding: Average ASR rose only from about 36.7 to 40.2, and BoolQ fine-tuning gave about 34.1, below base.

relationships.reason: Average ASR is essentially unchanged (~23.1 vs ~23.7). AdvBench falls 28.85→27.45, and AG News fine-tuning lowers all three ASRs (Table 1; missing row, verdict from text).
relationships.display_finding: Average attack success was essentially unchanged at about 23.1 versus 23.7, AdvBench fell from 28.85 to 27.45, and AG News fine-tuning lowered all three attack success rates.

relationships.reason: The rise is small in absolute terms (56→80 of 2,400, ~1 point), so effect size depends on the judge (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Unsafe outputs rose from 56 to 80 of 2,400, about 1 point in absolute terms, so effect size depended on the judge.
